arise.gloss: To come up or come into being — of problems, questions, and opportunities; in formal or older use, to get up.

senses.head: Come up, occur (of a situation)
senses.body: The everyday sense: questions, problems, needs, and opportunities *arise*. It never takes an object — you *raise* a question, but a question *arises*.
examples: Questions *arise* every time the budget changes midyear.
A dispute *arose* over who owned the fence.
New evidence *has arisen* since the trial began.
If the need *arises*, call me at home.

senses.head: Arise from, arise out of
senses.body: With *from* or *out of*: to have something as its cause or origin. Standard in formal, legal, and academic writing.
examples: Most complaints *arise* from a single billing error.
The lawsuit *arose* out of a contract signed in 1998.
Several claims *have arisen* from the same accident.

senses.head: Get up, rise (formal)
senses.body: Literary and elevated — standing up, or getting out of bed. Ordinary American speech uses *get up*.
examples: The congregation *arises* for the final hymn.
He *arose* before dawn and made coffee in the dark.
She *had arisen* early every day of that long summer.

befall.gloss: To happen to someone, nearly always something unwelcome.

senses.head: Happen to someone (something bad)
senses.body: Formal and literary. Unlike plain *fall* it takes a person or a place as its object, and what befalls is misfortune — trouble, disaster, harm.
examples: Whatever troubles *befall* us, we handle them together.
A string of disasters *befell* the company that winter.
Nothing like this *has befallen* the town in living memory.
He wondered what *had befallen* the crew of the second boat.
Misfortune *befalls* the careless traveler.

senses.head: Come to pass (archaic)
senses.body: The older objectless use, meaning simply *to happen*. Found in scripture and folktale, not in current American speech.
examples: It *befell* on the third night that the gate stood open.
Strange things *have befallen* since the comet passed.

bequeath.gloss: To leave property to someone in a will, and by extension to pass anything on to those who come after you.

senses.head: Leave in a will
senses.body: The legal sense, used of money and personal property. In modern American English the verb is regular: *bequeathed*, *have bequeathed*.
examples: Wealthy donors often *bequeath* their libraries to a university.
Her will *bequeathed* the house to her sister, not to her son.
The family *has bequeathed* three paintings to the museum since 1980.
He *bequeaths* nothing to anyone who contests the estate.

senses.head: Hand down to later generations
senses.body: Figurative: to leave something non-material — a legacy, a problem, a body of work — to whoever comes next.
examples: Each administration *bequeaths* its unfinished business to the next.
That century *bequeathed* us both the vaccine and the bomb.
Their teachers *have bequeathed* them a whole vocabulary for it.

senses.head: Strong forms bequoth, bequothen (archaic)
senses.body: The strong inflection listed for this verb survives only in old wills and literary imitations of them. Do not use it in anything you write today.
examples: The parish record says the merchant *bequoth* his lands to the abbey.
Scholars still argue over what the founder *had bequothen* to the town.

bestride.gloss: To sit or stand with a leg on either side of something; figuratively, to dominate an entire field.

senses.head: Dominate, tower over
senses.body: The sense still in use, and always literary or journalistic: one firm or figure *bestrides* an industry or an era.
examples: That one company *has bestridden* the industry for twenty years.
A single firm now *bestrides* the entire market.
By 1900 the railroads *had bestridden* the continent.

senses.head: Sit or stand astride
senses.body: The literal sense — a leg on each side of a horse, a log, or a wall. Ordinary American speech says *sit astride* instead.
examples: Bronze generals *bestride* half the squares in Europe.
He *bestrode* the fallen log and pulled the rope tight.
The rider *bestrode* a gray mare and led the parade.

senses.head: Step across, span
senses.body: Rare and old: to cross something in a single stride, or of a structure to span it.
examples: A stone causeway lets you *bestride* the stream without wading.
The arch *bestrode* the whole road until 1912.

bid.gloss: To offer a price, at auction or for a contract; in an older and more formal sense, to command, to greet, or to invite.

senses.head: Offer a price at auction
senses.body: In this sense the verb never changes shape: *bid, bid, bid*. Not *he bade forty dollars*.
examples: Two collectors *bid* against each other for the manuscript.
She *bid* nine hundred dollars and got the table.
Three people *have bid* on that lamp already.

senses.head: Bid on / bid for a contract
senses.body: Business use with *on* or *for*: to submit a formal offer to do work at a stated price. The forms stay invariant here too.
examples: Small contractors rarely *bid* on federal jobs.
They *bid* too low and lost money on the project.
The city *had bid* for the tournament twice before.

senses.head: Command, tell someone to do
senses.body: Formal and literary — this is the sense that carries the strong forms *bade* and *bidden*. It takes a bare infinitive: *bid them come in*.
examples: He *bids* his students think for themselves.
The sergeant *bade* them wait outside the tent.
The captain *has bidden* the crew to stand down.

senses.head: Bid farewell, bid good night
senses.body: A fixed formula for greetings and farewells: *bid someone welcome, farewell, good night*. Most Americans say *bade* as /bæd/, rhyming with *had*.
examples: She *bade* us good night and went upstairs.
We *bade* farewell at the gate and drove home.
They *have bidden* their guests welcome in three languages.

senses.head: Invite (archaic)
senses.body: Old use, alive today mostly in the phrase *the bidden guests*. Modern English uses *invite*.
examples: The steward *bade* the whole village to the wedding.
The host *had bidden* the guests to arrive at seven.
Only those *bidden* to the feast came through the gate.

blow.gloss: Of air, to move or to move something; of a person, to force air out of the mouth — plus a large family of idioms from *blow up* to *blow it*.

senses.head: Of wind: move, be in motion
senses.body: The core intransitive sense, with wind or a draft as the subject.
examples: Cold winds *blow* off the lake all winter.
It *blew* hard all night.
The wind *has blown* from the south since Tuesday.

senses.head: Move something with air
senses.body: Transitive: air moves an object, usually with a particle — *blow off, blow over, blow away*.
examples: Papers *blow* everywhere when that door opens.
The storm *blew* three shingles off the roof.
A gust *has blown* the umbrella into the pool.

senses.head: Breathe out forcefully
senses.body: Of a person directing breath at something. This covers the fixed *blow out the candles* and *blow your nose*.
examples: She *blows* on her coffee to cool it.
He *blew* out all the candles at once.
*Blow* your nose before you come to the table.
The nurse asked whether he *had blown* into the tube yet.

senses.head: Sound a horn or a whistle
senses.body: Used of wind instruments, whistles, and car horns. The related noun *whistleblower* comes from this sense.
examples: Conductors *blow* the whistle before the doors close.
The referee *blew* the whistle on the play.
Someone *has blown* the horn three times.

senses.head: Blow up — explode; destroy
senses.body: Both transitive and intransitive. *Blow up* also means to lose your temper, and, recently, for something to become suddenly popular.
examples: Engineers plan to *blow up* the old bridge in March.
The transformer *blew up* during the storm.
The video *has blown up* on every platform.

senses.head: Burn out, burst (a fuse, a tire)
senses.body: Of something that fails suddenly under pressure or current. Works in both directions: *the fuse blew*, *he blew the fuse*.
examples: Cheap bulbs *blow* within a month.
The rear tire *blew* on the interstate.
Somebody *has blown* the fuse again.

senses.head: Waste, squander (money)
senses.body: Informal, with money or time as the object, often with *on* or *through*.
examples: Do not *blow* your whole budget in the first week.
He *blew* an entire paycheck on concert tickets.
They *have blown* through the grant already.

senses.head: Blow it — ruin a chance
senses.body: Informal. The object is an opportunity: a game, an interview, a lead.
examples: Do not *blow* this.
He *blew* the interview by showing up late.
We *have blown* two chances at the title.

senses.head: Blow off — skip, brush aside
senses.body: Informal: to skip an obligation, or to dismiss a person or a concern without taking it seriously.
examples: He *blows off* class whenever the surf is good.
She *blew off* the whole warning.
He *has blown off* three appointments this month.

senses.head: Blow over — pass without consequence
senses.body: Of a storm, a scandal, or an argument that ends without lasting damage.
examples: Stories like this usually *blow over*.
The whole thing *blew over* in a week.
The controversy *had blown over* long before he got back.

co-write.gloss: To write something jointly with another person.

senses.head: Write jointly with someone
senses.body: Standard for songs, screenplays, books, and papers; the collaborator follows *with*. American style keeps the hyphen and stresses the second part.
examples: The two friends *co-write* every song on the album.
She *co-wrote* the screenplay with her brother.
He *has co-written* four textbooks with the same colleague.
The report *had been co-written* by two agencies.
He *co-writes* a column with a retired judge.
They *co-wrote* the grant proposal in a single weekend.

crow.gloss: Of a rooster, to make its loud call; of a person, to boast about a win.

senses.head: Boast, gloat
senses.body: The everyday sense, mildly disapproving, usually *crow about* or *crow over*. Regular in modern American English: *crowed*, *have crowed*.
examples: She *crows* whenever her team wins.
He *crowed* about the promotion for a solid week.
They *have crowed* about that one game for years.

senses.head: Of a rooster: call
senses.body: The literal sense. The strong past *crew* survives only in older and biblical English, and the participle *crown* is obsolete — use *crowed* today.
examples: The roosters *crow* before the sun clears the ridge.
Their rooster *has crowed* every morning since April.
The old translation reads that the cock *crew* three times.
Antique printings of the ballad say the cock *had crown* twice before daybreak.

senses.head: Of a baby: squeal with delight
senses.body: A small, affectionate use: the happy noise an infant makes.
examples: Babies *crow* when you lift them overhead.
The baby *crowed* and reached for the balloon.
He *has crowed* and giggled all morning.

do.gloss: To perform an action or a task — and, as an auxiliary, the verb that carries tense in questions, negatives, and emphasis.

senses.head: Perform, carry out
senses.body: The core lexical sense, with a task, a job, or a chore as the object. Not *I done it*: the participle always needs *have*.
examples: We *do* the dishes right after dinner.
She *did* the whole route on foot.
He *has done* more than anyone asked him to.
By noon they *had done* half the packing.

senses.head: Auxiliary in questions and negatives
senses.body: *Do* carries the tense so the main verb stays in the base form. That is why *did you went* is wrong and *did you go* is right.
examples: *Do* you take cream?
She *did* not answer the second email.
*Does* he know about the meeting?

senses.head: Emphatic do
senses.body: Stressed *do* in an affirmative sentence insists on it against doubt or contradiction.
examples: I *do* remember her name — give me a second.
He *did* apologize, eventually.
She *does* care, whatever she says.

senses.head: Stand in for another verb
senses.body: *Do* substitutes for a verb already mentioned, especially in comparisons, short answers, and tag questions.
examples: She reads more than I *do*.
He said he would call, and he *did*.
Nobody *has done* more for this town than she has.

senses.head: Tidy, arrange, put in order
senses.body: *Do* a room, *do* your hair, *do* the yard — to put something into the state it is supposed to be in.
examples: She *does* her hair before anyone else is awake.
They *did* the whole kitchen over a weekend.
The cleaners *have done* the upstairs already.

senses.head: Be enough, suffice
senses.body: Intransitive, usually with *will* or *would*: *that will do*, *it will do for now*.
examples: Two chairs will *do* for now.
A shorter rope *did* just fine.
Cold pizza *has done* the job before.

senses.head: Fare, get along
senses.body: Always with an adverb — *doing well*, *doing badly*, *how are you doing*. Standard in talk about health and business alike.
examples: How *did* she *do* on the exam?
The store *did* badly its first year.
She *has done* well for herself.

senses.head: Cover a distance or a speed
senses.body: With a measurement as the object: miles covered, miles per gallon, speed on the highway.
examples: This car *does* thirty miles to the gallon.
We *did* four hundred miles before dark.
They *had done* the whole loop by noon.

senses.head: Serve a prison sentence
senses.body: Informal but widespread: *do time*, *do five years*.
examples: Nobody wants to *do* a day in that place.
He *did* eight years upstate.
She *has done* time for fraud.

senses.head: Do over — redo from the start
senses.body: American English keeps *do over* where British English says *do again*; a *do-over* is also a noun.
examples: The teacher made him *do* the essay *over*.
We *did* the bathroom *over* last spring.
They *have done* the whole website *over* twice.

senses.head: Do without / could do with
senses.body: *Do without* means to manage in the absence of something; *could do with* means to need or want it.
examples: We can *do* without a second car.
They *did* without heat for three days.
She *has done* without help all year.
I could *do* with a nap.

senses.head: Do away with — abolish
senses.body: To get rid of a rule, a practice, or an institution for good.
examples: Nobody wants to *do away with* the program.
The district *did away with* letter grades.
They *have done away with* the paper form entirely.

draw.gloss: To make a picture with lines; to pull; and, by extension, to attract, to take out, and to end level.

senses.head: Make a picture, sketch
senses.body: The most common sense, of lines made by hand rather than paint or color.
examples: Architects still *draw* by hand for the first sketches.
She *drew* a map on the back of the receipt.
He *has drawn* the same barn a hundred times.

senses.head: Pull, drag
senses.body: Somewhat formal for plain pulling, but ordinary in fixed uses: *draw the curtains*, *draw a chair up*, *horses draw a wagon*.
examples: Two horses *draw* the wagon up the hill.
He *drew* the chair closer to the fire.
The curtains *had been drawn* before we arrived.

senses.head: Attract
senses.body: Of crowds, attention, criticism, or interest — what the subject pulls toward itself.
examples: Free food *draws* a crowd every time.
Her first novel *drew* attention from three publishers.
The exhibit *has drawn* record crowds.

senses.head: Take out, withdraw
senses.body: Of money from an account, a card from a deck, a weapon from a holster, or water from a well.
examples: You can *draw* cash at any branch.
He *drew* a card from the top of the deck.
She *has drawn* her salary from the same account for years.

senses.head: Draw a conclusion, a comparison, a line
senses.body: A fixed set of abstract objects: conclusions, distinctions, parallels, and the line you will not cross.
examples: Do not *draw* conclusions from one bad week.
The report *drew* a sharp comparison with 2008.
Critics *have drawn* the obvious parallel.

senses.head: Draw blood, draw a breath
senses.body: Two set collocations: taking blood for a test or a wound, and taking in air.
examples: A nurse will *draw* blood before the appointment.
He *drew* a long breath and started over.
They *have drawn* blood twice this week.

senses.head: End level, tie (sports, chess)
senses.body: Standard in soccer and chess; in most American sports the ordinary verb is *tie*, though the noun *a draw* is used everywhere.
examples: The two grandmasters usually *draw* when they meet.
United *drew* with City on Saturday.
They *have drawn* three matches in a row.

senses.head: Draw up — compose a document
senses.body: Of contracts, wills, plans, and lists put together in written form.
examples: We should *draw up* a list before we shop.
The lawyer *drew up* the contract overnight.
The committee *has drawn up* new rules.

senses.head: Draw on / draw upon — use as a resource
senses.body: To take material, money, or experience from a source you already have.
examples: Good teachers *draw on* their own mistakes.
The novel *drew* heavily *on* her childhood.
He *has drawn on* that fund twice.

senses.head: Draw out — prolong; get someone talking
senses.body: Two related uses: making something last too long, and coaxing a quiet person into conversation.
examples: Do not *draw* the meeting *out*.
She *drew* him *out* with a few easy questions.
The negotiations *have been drawn out* for months.

senses.head: Draw near, draw to a close
senses.body: Of time approaching. Slightly formal, common in writing and speeches.
examples: Winter *draws* near.
The year *drew* to a close without a deal.
The season *has drawn* to a close.

drive.gloss: To operate a vehicle; to force someone or something into a state; and to power, push, or propel.

senses.head: Operate a vehicle
senses.body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. Not *I have drove* — the participle is *driven*.
examples: I *drive* to the coast every August.
He *drove* nine hours without stopping.
She *has driven* that truck since college.

senses.head: Take someone somewhere by car
senses.body: With a person as the object: you drive them, and the destination follows.
examples: I can *drive* you to the airport.
My neighbor *drove* us home after the game.
He *has driven* her to every appointment.

senses.head: Force into a state or an action
senses.body: *Drive someone crazy*, *drive prices up*, *drive families out* — the subject pushes the object into a condition it did not choose.
examples: The noise *drives* me crazy.
Debt *drove* him to sell the shop.
High rents *have driven* young families out of the city.

senses.head: Power, propel (a machine)
senses.body: Of the energy source behind machinery. Often passive: *the pump is driven by a small motor*.
examples: A small motor *drives* the belt.
Steam *drove* the first looms.
The pumps *have been driven* by solar panels since June.

senses.head: Motivate, be the force behind
senses.body: With an abstract subject — curiosity, fear, cheap credit. The participle is a common adjective for an ambitious person: *a driven student*.
examples: Curiosity *drives* most of her work.
Fear *drove* the whole campaign.
Cheap credit *has driven* the boom.

senses.head: Hammer in, force in
senses.body: Of nails, stakes, posts, and screws forced into place by repeated blows.
examples: *Drive* the stake in at an angle.
He *drove* the last nail at sunset.
They *have driven* posts along the whole fence line.

senses.head: Herd animals
senses.body: The old sense that gives us *cattle drive* and *drover*.
examples: Ranchers still *drive* cattle to summer pasture.
The crew *drove* the herd across the shallow ford.
Cowboys *had driven* the steers north for weeks.

senses.head: Hit hard (golf, baseball)
senses.body: Sports use: a long, hard hit. *Drive in a run* is standard baseball, and the noun *RBI* comes from it.
examples: He can *drive* a ball three hundred yards.
She *drove* a single into right field.
He *has driven* in four runs tonight.

senses.head: Drive at — mean, be getting at
senses.body: Almost always in the progressive and almost always in a question about what someone really means.
examples: What are you *driving at*?
I could not tell what he *was driving at*.
Nobody knew what she *had been driving at* until later.

eat.gloss: To take food into the mouth and swallow it; also, to wear away, and the base of several everyday idioms.

senses.head: Consume food
senses.body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. The participle never stands alone: not *I eaten already* but *I have eaten already*.
examples: We *eat* dinner around seven.
He *ate* two bowls of chili and asked for more.
The kids *have eaten* already.
By the time I sat down, they *had eaten* every roll.

senses.head: Eat out / eat in — take a meal
senses.body: *Eat out* means at a restaurant, *eat in* means at home. Both are fixed and cannot be reversed.
examples: We *eat out* twice a week.
They *ate in* every night that month.
She *has eaten* lunch at her desk since March.

senses.head: Eat up — consume entirely
senses.body: Literal with food, and very common with time and money as the object.
examples: Rent *eats up* half her paycheck.
The delay *ate up* the whole morning.
Legal fees *have eaten up* the settlement.

senses.head: Eat into, eat away — corrode
senses.body: Of acid, rust, salt, or water gradually destroying a surface, and of costs gradually destroying a margin.
examples: Salt *eats into* the underside of the car.
The river *ate away* four feet of bank.
Rust *has eaten* through the pan.

senses.head: Bother, trouble (what is eating you)
senses.body: Informal, usually progressive or with *at*: something is quietly bothering a person.
examples: Something *is eating* him and he will not say what.
What *ate* at her all week was the silence.
Guilt *has eaten* at him since the trial.

senses.head: Eat one's words
senses.body: A fixed phrase: to be forced to admit that what you said confidently was wrong.
examples: He had to *eat* his words by Friday.
She *ate* her words on live television.
They *have eaten* those words more than once.

fall.gloss: To drop toward the ground; to decrease; to pass into a state; and, of cities and governments, to be defeated.

senses.head: Drop toward the ground
senses.body: The core sense, and it never takes an object: not *he fell the glass* but *he dropped the glass*.
examples: Leaves *fall* early up in the mountains.
He *fell* off the ladder and broke his wrist.
Snow *had fallen* all night on the pass.
The old barn *has fallen* in on itself.

senses.head: Decrease, go down
senses.body: Of prices, temperatures, numbers, and rates. The opposite is *rise*, not *raise*.
examples: Prices *fall* after the holidays.
The temperature *fell* twenty degrees in an hour.
Enrollment *has fallen* for three straight years.

senses.head: Pass into a state — fall asleep, fall ill
senses.ru: впадать в состояние: заснуть, заболеть, влюбиться
senses.body: A fixed pattern with a short list of complements: *asleep, ill, silent, in love, behind on payments*.
examples: She *falls* asleep on every flight.
He *fell* in love with the town on the first visit.
Half the crew *has fallen* ill.

senses.head: Be captured or defeated
senses.body: Of cities, fortresses, and governments that lose power or are taken by an enemy.
examples: Cities like that rarely *fall* without a siege.
The capital *fell* in three days.
The government *had fallen* before the vote was counted.

senses.head: Die in battle
senses.body: Formal and commemorative. *The fallen* is the standard collective noun for soldiers killed in war.
examples: Soldiers *fall* and towns forget them.
Thousands *fell* on that ridge.
Men *have fallen* here in two wars.

senses.head: Occur on a date
senses.body: Of holidays, deadlines, and anniversaries landing on a particular day.
examples: Thanksgiving *falls* late this year.
My birthday *fell* on a Monday.
The deadline *has fallen* on a holiday twice now.

senses.head: Fall apart — break down, collapse
senses.body: Literal for objects, figurative for deals, plans, and people who stop coping.
examples: Cheap furniture *falls apart* in a year.
The deal *fell apart* over money.
He *has fallen apart* since the diagnosis.

senses.head: Fall behind — lag
senses.body: With *on* or *with*: to be later or further back than you should be, often about work or payments.
examples: Try not to *fall behind* on the reading.
They *fell behind* on the rent in March.
She *has fallen behind* two chapters.

senses.head: Fall through — fail to happen
senses.body: Of an arrangement that collapses before it is completed.
examples: Plans like that often *fall through*.
The sale *fell through* at the last minute.
Two offers *have fallen through* already.

senses.head: Fall for — be taken in by
senses.body: Informal: to be fooled by a trick or a lie you should have seen through.
examples: People still *fall for* that email.
He *fell for* the oldest trick in the book.
I *have fallen for* worse scams.

senses.head: Fall back on — resort to
senses.body: Of the reserve you turn to when the first choice fails: savings, an old job, a familiar excuse.
examples: It helps to have savings to *fall back on*.
She *fell back on* her old job.
They *have fallen back on* the same excuse all year.

fly.gloss: To move through the air; to travel in or pilot an aircraft; and, of time and people, to move very fast.

senses.head: Move through the air
senses.body: The core sense, of birds, insects, and anything airborne.
examples: Geese *fly* south along the river every October.
A hawk *flew* low over the field.
Sparks *have flown* into the dry grass.

senses.head: Travel by plane
senses.body: Of the passenger rather than the pilot. Not *I have flew* — the participle is *flown*.
examples: I *fly* out Sunday night.
We *flew* to Denver on Tuesday morning.
She *has flown* this route a hundred times.

senses.head: Pilot an aircraft
senses.body: Transitive, with the aircraft as the object: *fly a plane*, *fly cargo*.
examples: She *flies* cargo runs to Alaska.
The copilot *flew* the last leg.
He *has flown* small planes since he was nineteen.

senses.head: Move fast, rush by
senses.body: Very common with time as the subject: *time flies*, *the week flew by*.
examples: Time *flies* when the work is interesting.
The morning *flew* by.
The whole week *has flown* past.

senses.head: Fly a flag, fly a kite
senses.body: Transitive, of something held up in the wind — a flag, a kite, a banner.
examples: Ships *fly* the flag of the country they are registered in.
Kids *flew* kites all afternoon out on the point.
The embassy *has flown* the flag at half staff all week.

senses.head: Flee, get away
senses.body: Literary and legal, and old-fashioned in speech; ordinary English uses *flee, fled*.
examples: Families *fly* the city at the first sign of trouble.
He *flew* the country before the indictment.
Many *have flown* to the hills for safety.

senses.head: Fly off the handle — lose your temper
senses.body: Informal and fixed; the *handle* never varies.
examples: He *flies off the handle* over nothing.
She *flew off the handle* at the dispatcher.
He *has flown off the handle* twice this week.

senses.head: Baseball: hit a fly ball
senses.body: In this sense only, the verb is regular: *flied out*, never *flew out*.
examples: He tends to *fly* out to left.
She *flied* out to end the inning.
The cleanup hitter *has flied* out three times tonight.

forbid.gloss: To order that something not be done.

senses.head: Order someone not to do something
senses.body: With a personal object plus *to* or *from* — *forbade him to leave*, *forbade him from leaving* — but never a bare infinitive.
examples: Parents who *forbid* everything get obeyed least.
The judge *forbade* any contact with the witness.
Her doctor *had forbidden* coffee for a month.

senses.head: Of a rule or law: prohibit
senses.body: With an inanimate subject — a rule, a lease, a statute — and usually no personal object at all.
examples: Most parks *forbid* open fires in August.
State law *forbade* the sale outright.
The lease *has forbidden* subletting from the start.

senses.head: God forbid, heaven forbid
senses.body: A frozen exclamation using the old subjunctive; the verb takes no other form inside it.
examples: God *forbid* anything happens to that bridge.
Heaven *forbid* she find out from a stranger.

foresee.gloss: To know or expect in advance that something will happen.

senses.head: Predict, expect in advance
senses.body: Of trends, outcomes, and events. Often negative: *nobody foresaw*, *no one could have foreseen*.
examples: Few economists *foresee* a sharp drop this year.
Nobody *foresaw* how fast the neighborhood would change.
We *have foreseen* most of these problems.
She *foresees* trouble with the schedule.

senses.head: Anticipate and plan for
senses.body: Engineering and legal use, where the adjective *foreseeable* does much of the work: *the foreseeable future*, *foreseeable risk*.
examples: Good contracts *foresee* the obvious disputes.
The engineers *had foreseen* the flaw but were overruled.
No one *had foreseen* a delay that long.

forgive.gloss: To stop being angry at someone for what they did; in finance, to cancel a debt.

senses.head: Pardon, stop being angry
senses.body: The core sense. You forgive a person, or you forgive the person for the act: *forgive him for lying*.
examples: Some people *forgive* easily; others never do.
She *forgave* him after a long talk on the porch.
I *have forgiven* worse than that.
My grandmother *forgives* everyone but the phone company.

senses.head: Cancel a debt
senses.body: Financial and quite literal: the money no longer has to be repaid. *Loan forgiveness* is the standard noun.
examples: The program *forgives* the balance after ten years of payments.
He *had forgiven* the debt years earlier.
The bank *has forgiven* part of the loan.

senses.head: Forgive me — polite formula
senses.body: A set softener before an interruption, a blunt question, or an apology for a mess.
examples: *Forgive* me for asking, but how much did it cost?
You will *forgive* the mess — we just moved in.

forsake.gloss: To abandon someone or something completely.

senses.head: Abandon a person
senses.body: Formal and literary, common in hymns and vows. Everyday American speech says *abandon* or *walk out on*.
examples: Good friends do not *forsake* you when things go wrong.
The old hymn says he never *forsakes* his people.
Her sons *had forsaken* the farm long before she died.

senses.head: Give up a place, habit, or plan
senses.body: With a thing rather than a person. The participle also works as a plain adjective: *a forsaken little town*.
examples: He *forsook* the city for a cabin in Maine.
She *has forsaken* sugar entirely.
The settlers *had forsaken* the valley by 1890.
They *have forsaken* a plan they spent a year building.

give.gloss: To hand something over or provide it — plus a large family of idioms from *give up* to *give birth*.

senses.head: Hand over, pass to someone
senses.body: The core sense, with two objects: *give someone something* or *give something to someone*.
examples: They *give* every new hire a week of training.
He *gave* me his number on a napkin.
She *has given* me the keys already.

senses.head: Donate, contribute
senses.body: Of charity and gifts, often intransitive with *to*: *give to the fund*.
examples: Alumni *give* to the scholarship fund every spring.
They *gave* ten thousand dollars to the shelter.
We *have given* away most of the furniture.

senses.head: Provide, cause someone to have
senses.body: *Give someone trouble, a headache, an idea, a hard time* — the subject causes the object to have something, good or bad.
examples: Cheap tires *give* you nothing but trouble.
The noise *gave* me a headache.
That trip *has given* her a whole new plan.

senses.head: Give a talk, a party, a performance
senses.body: With an event as the object: the subject is the one putting it on.
examples: She *gives* the same talk twice a year.
They *gave* a party for the retiring dean.
He *has given* four concerts this month.

senses.head: Yield, bend under pressure
senses.body: Intransitive: something bends, stretches, or breaks rather than holding firm.
examples: The old lock *gives* if you push hard.
The floorboard *gave* under his weight.
The rope *had given* before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Give up — stop trying; surrender
senses.body: Two branches: to quit an effort, and to quit a habit. *Give oneself up* is to surrender to the police.
examples: Do not *give up* this early.
He *gave up* smoking in his forties.
She *has given up* on the whole project.

senses.head: Give in — yield to pressure
senses.body: To stop resisting a demand, usually after holding out for a while. Often with *to*.
examples: Parents *give in* faster than they admit.
The union *gave in* on the pension question.
Management *has given in* twice already.

senses.head: Give out — run out; distribute; fail
senses.body: Three related uses: supplies run out, people hand things out, and bodies or machines quit working.
examples: Volunteers *give out* water at every mile.
The batteries *gave out* halfway through.
His knees *have given out*.

senses.head: Give away — donate; reveal
senses.body: To hand over for nothing, or to let a secret slip. *Give away the ending* is the standard spoiler warning.
examples: The store *gives away* samples on Saturdays.
His face *gave* him *away*.
Somebody *has given away* the ending.

senses.head: Give birth
senses.body: A fixed phrase, with *to* before the child. Also figurative: *the era gave birth to a whole style*.
examples: Cows on this farm *give birth* in early spring.
She *gave birth* on the way to the hospital.
She *has given birth* to three boys.

senses.head: Given — considering, in view of
senses.body: The participle has hardened into a preposition and conjunction: *given the weather*, *given that we are late*.
examples: *Given* the weather, the turnout was good.
*Given that* nobody objected, we moved on.

grow.gloss: To get bigger over time, to cultivate something that does, and to become — gradually — something else.

senses.head: Get bigger, increase
senses.body: The core intransitive sense, of people, towns, numbers, and anything that gets larger on its own.
examples: Cities *grow* toward the water first.
He *grew* four inches over the summer.
The town *has grown* by half since 2010.

senses.head: Cultivate, raise (plants)
senses.body: Transitive, with a crop or a plant as the object.
examples: Tomatoes *grow* well on that side of the house.
She *grows* herbs on the fire escape.
They *have grown* the same corn for forty years.

senses.head: Let hair or a beard get longer
senses.body: Transitive, often with *out*: *grow it out*.
examples: He decided to *grow* a beard in November.
Her hair *had grown* past her shoulders.
She *has grown* it out twice and cut it both times.

senses.head: Become, turn gradually
senses.body: With an adjective: *grow quiet, grow tired, grow dark*. Slightly more formal and slower-sounding than *get*.
examples: People *grow* impatient in that line.
It *grew* dark before we reached the car.
The crowd *has grown* quiet.

senses.head: Expand a business
senses.body: Transitive and firmly business register: *grow the company*, *grow revenue*. Some editors still dislike it.
examples: They want to *grow* the company without new debt.
She *grew* the client list from six to sixty.
He *has grown* revenue every quarter.

senses.head: Grow up — become an adult
senses.body: Both about maturing and about where your childhood happened: *I grew up two towns over*.
examples: Kids *grow up* fast around here.
I *grew up* two towns over.
He *has grown up* a lot since the fall.

senses.head: Grow on someone — become likable
senses.body: Of something you disliked at first and came to enjoy. The subject is the thing, not the person.
examples: The song *grows on* you.
The apartment *grew on* her by August.
That painting *has grown on* me.

senses.head: Grow apart, grow into
senses.ru: отдаляться друг от друга; дорасти до
senses.body: *Grow apart* is of relationships that fade; *grow into* is of a role or a piece of clothing you become the right size for.
examples: Old friends sometimes *grow apart*.
They *grew apart* after the move.
He *has grown into* the job.

know.gloss: To have information about something, to be acquainted with someone, and to be able to tell one thing from another.

senses.head: Have information, be aware
senses.body: The core sense, with a clause or a fact as the object. Not a progressive verb: not *I am knowing*.
examples: They *know* the neighborhood better than anyone.
I *knew* the answer and then forgot it.
We *had known* about the layoffs for weeks.

senses.head: Be acquainted with a person or place
senses.body: Of people, cities, and streets you have direct experience of, usually with *since* or *for*.
examples: Do you *know* the family on the corner?
He *knew* the city well enough to skip the map.
She *has known* him since grade school.

senses.head: Have a skill, know how to
senses.body: *Know how to* plus a verb, or *know* a language or a trade.
examples: He *knows* three languages.
She *knew* how to fix the pump herself.
Nobody here *has known* how to run that machine since he left.

senses.head: Recognize, tell apart
senses.body: Often *know someone by* a detail, or *know A from B*.
examples: You would *know* her anywhere by that laugh.
I *knew* him from his voice before he turned around.
He *has known* good work from bad since he was twenty.

senses.head: Experience, live through
senses.body: Usually in the perfect and often negative: *she has never known hunger*. Formal and a little literary.
examples: Few of us *know* what that is like.
He *knew* real poverty as a child.
That family *has never known* a quiet year.

senses.head: Know of, know about
senses.body: Weaker than plain *know*: to have heard of something without direct acquaintance.
examples: I *know of* her, but we have never met.
Nobody *knew about* the second offer.
The board *has known about* the deficit since spring.

senses.head: Be known as, be known for
senses.body: Passive only. *Known as* gives a name or role; *known for* gives what something is famous for.
examples: The street *is known* for its bakeries.
He *was known* around town as Doc.
The place *has been known* by three names.

lie.gloss: To be, or move into, a flat resting position; also, to be situated, and to consist in something. (The verb meaning *to tell an untruth* is a separate, regular verb: *lied, lied*.)

senses.head: Recline, lie down
senses.body: Takes no object. The transitive twin *lay, laid, laid* means to put something down, which is why *I laid down for a nap* is the most common error in English — the right form is *I lay down*.
examples: I *lie* down for twenty minutes after lunch.
She *lay* on the couch all afternoon.
The keys *have lain* on the counter since Friday.
He *lay* awake until three in the morning.

senses.head: Be situated (of a place)
senses.body: Of towns, borders, and land relative to something else. Slightly formal but standard in description.
examples: The town *lies* just east of the river.
The border *lay* two hours north of the camp.
The ruins *have lain* under that field for centuries.

senses.head: Remain in a state — lie idle, lie empty
senses.body: With an adjective: something stays untouched or unused for a long stretch.
examples: Half the lots *lie* empty.
The mill *lay* idle for a decade.
Snow *had lain* on the field for a week.

senses.head: Lie in, lie with — consist in; rest with
senses.body: Formal: *the problem lies in the wiring*, *the decision lies with the board*.
examples: The trouble *lies* in the wiring, not the switch.
The final say *lay* with the trustees.
The answer *has lain* in the data all along.

senses.head: Lie ahead, lie behind
senses.body: Of what is coming and of what caused something, both common in narrative and news writing.
examples: A hard winter *lies* ahead.
Nobody knew what *lay* behind the decision.
Whatever *had lain* behind the delay, no one explained it.

mistake.gloss: To take one person or thing to be another, and so to be wrong about it.

senses.head: Mistake A for B
senses.body: The pattern is *mistake A for B*, never *mistake A with B*.
examples: People often *mistake* her for her sister.
I *mistook* the salt for sugar.
He *has mistaken* my silence for agreement.
Nobody *mistakes* him for a beginner anymore.

senses.head: Be mistaken — be wrong
senses.body: A passive-shaped fixed use where the participle is really an adjective: *you are mistaken*, *if I am not mistaken*.
examples: You *are mistaken* about the deadline.
If I *am not mistaken*, she left at six.
He admitted he *had been mistaken*.

senses.head: There is no mistaking
senses.body: A frozen negative construction meaning something is unmistakable.
examples: There is no *mistaking* that voice.
There was no *mistaking* what he meant.
She *had mistaken* the date and arrived a day early, but there was no *mistaking* the invitation.

outdo.gloss: To do something better than someone else does it.

senses.head: Surpass, do better than
senses.body: With a rival or a previous version as the object.
examples: The brothers try to *outdo* each other every Thanksgiving.
Nobody *outdoes* him at trivia night.
The sequel *has outdone* the original at the box office.
They *had outdone* every rival by June.

senses.head: Outdo oneself
senses.body: Reflexive and always a compliment: to do unusually well by your own standard.
examples: She *outdid* herself with the cake this year.
You have really *outdone* yourself.
He *outdoes* himself every holiday.

senses.head: Not to be outdone
senses.body: A frozen phrase that introduces whoever answers a display in kind.
examples: Not to be *outdone*, the other store cut its prices too.
The neighbors, not to be *outdone*, *outdid* the whole block with lights.

outgrow.gloss: To grow too big or too old for something, or to grow faster than something else.

senses.head: Grow too big for (clothes)
senses.body: The everyday sense, about children and clothing. It always takes an object.
examples: Kids *outgrow* shoes faster than they wear them out.
My son *outgrows* his jeans every spring.
She *has outgrown* every coat we bought her.

senses.head: Grow out of a habit or a fear
senses.body: Of a phase, an allergy, or a fear that goes away as a person gets older.
examples: Most children *outgrow* the allergy.
He *outgrew* his fear of dogs.
She *has outgrown* the tantrums.

senses.head: Become too big for a place or system
senses.body: Of an organization that no longer fits its building, its tools, or its structure.
examples: A school *outgrows* its building faster than the district plans for.
The company *had outgrown* its first office within a year.
They *have outgrown* the old scheduling system.

senses.head: Grow faster than something else
senses.body: Comparative use with two things growing at once — demand against supply, suburbs against the city.
examples: The suburbs *outgrew* the city in a decade.
Demand *has outgrown* supply.
Costs regularly *outgrow* the budget that set them.

overdo.gloss: To do something to excess — and, of food, to cook it too long.

senses.head: Do to excess
senses.body: Very often the fixed *overdo it*, especially about effort and exercise.
examples: Do not *overdo* it on your first day back at the gym.
He always *overdoes* the apologies.
She *has overdone* the decorations this year.

senses.head: Use too much of an ingredient
senses.body: With the ingredient or element as the object: garlic, salt, cologne, exclamation points.
examples: He *overdid* the garlic again.
They *had overdone* the salt in the second batch.
Editors *overdo* the italics in that series.

senses.head: Overcook
senses.body: Usually met as the participle used adjectivally: *an overdone steak*.
examples: Do not *overdo* the roast — pull it at 130.
The cook *had overdone* the steak.
Every burger on the tray *has been overdone*.

senses.head: Overplay, exaggerate
senses.body: Of a performance, a script, or an effect pushed past what the material can carry.
examples: The actor *overdoes* every death scene.
The script *overdid* the sentiment.
Critics said the film *had overdone* the twist.

overdraw.gloss: To take more money out of an account than it holds; in criticism, to exaggerate a portrayal.

senses.head: Take out more than the balance
senses.ru: превысить остаток счёта, уйти в минус
senses.body: Banking, with the account as the object. The fee for it is an *overdraft*.
examples: Students often *overdraw* their checking accounts in the first month.
He *overdrew* the account by sixty dollars.
She *has overdrawn* twice this year.

senses.head: Be overdrawn (of an account)
senses.body: The passive and adjectival form, which is how most Americans actually meet the word.
examples: The account *was overdrawn* when the check cleared.
My balance *has been overdrawn* since Tuesday.
The app warns you before you *overdraw*.
They *had overdrawn* the account before payday.

senses.head: Exaggerate a portrayal
senses.body: Literary criticism: *an overdrawn character* is drawn too broadly to be believed.
examples: Beginning novelists *overdraw* their villains.
The playwright *overdrew* the father badly.
Every figure in the book *has been overdrawn*.

overeat.gloss: To eat more than you should.

senses.head: Eat too much
senses.body: It takes no object: not *I overate the pie* but *I ate too much pie*, or simply *I overate*.
examples: It is easy to *overeat* at a buffet.
We all *overate* at Thanksgiving.
He *has overeaten* every night this week.
She felt sick because she *had overeaten*.
My uncle *overeats* whenever he is bored.

overgrow.gloss: To cover something with growth; in practice, met almost only as the participle *overgrown*.

senses.head: Cover with growth
senses.body: Of vines, weeds, moss, and brush spreading over a surface. The plant is the subject, the place is the object.
examples: Vines *overgrow* the fence every summer.
Weeds *overgrew* the whole lot in two months.
Ivy *has overgrown* the north wall.
Brush *had overgrown* the trail long before we tried it.

senses.head: Overgrown as an adjective
senses.body: The living form of this verb: *an overgrown lot*, and figuratively *an overgrown puppy*, too big for its age.
examples: The yard was completely *overgrown*.
He is an *overgrown* kid with a mortgage.
The garden *has overgrown* since she moved out.

overlie.gloss: To lie on top of something else, most often a layer of rock, tissue, or material resting over another.

senses.head: Lie on top of, cover
senses.body: The everyday use is technical — geology, anatomy, materials — describing one layer sitting above another. It is transitive and almost never used of a person lying on a bed.
examples: Layers of sandstone *overlie* the coal seam throughout the valley.
A thin film of clay *overlay* the ash from the eruption.
Volcanic rock *has overlain* these deposits for millions of years.
The surveyors found that gravel *had overlain* the old roadbed.

senses.head: Smother by lying on
senses.body: A narrow, mostly historical and medical sense used of a parent or animal that suffocates an infant or a young animal by rolling onto it. You will meet it in old court records and veterinary writing, not in conversation.
examples: Coroners in that era often ruled that a mother *had overlain* her child in the night.
The sow *overlay* two of the piglets before dawn.
Farmers still build rails into the pen so that a sow cannot *overlie* her litter.

override.gloss: To set aside or take precedence over a decision, a rule, or an automatic control.

senses.head: Overrule a decision
senses.body: The core sense: a higher authority cancels a lower one. Standard in politics and business — Congress *overrides* a veto, a manager *overrides* a refund denial.
examples: The Senate can *override* a veto with a two-thirds vote.
The board *overrode* the committee's recommendation without much discussion.
Management *has overridden* the store policy twice this month.
By then the governor *had overridden* the county's own order.

senses.head: Take precedence over
senses.body: Used of one concern outweighing another. The subject is usually an abstract noun — safety, cost, loyalty.
examples: Safety concerns *override* the schedule every single time.
Her loyalty to the team *overrode* any interest in a bigger paycheck.
Convenience *has overridden* privacy in most of these apps.

senses.head: Take manual control of a system
senses.ru: переводить на ручное управление, отключать автоматику
senses.body: Technical: a person or a switch cancels what an automatic system was going to do. The noun *override* (a manual override) comes straight from this.
examples: You can *override* the thermostat from the panel in the hallway.
The pilot *overrode* the autopilot and landed the plane by hand.
Someone *had overridden* the alarm before the fire started.

senses.head: Override a method
senses.body: In object-oriented programming, to replace an inherited method with a new definition in a subclass. Everyday vocabulary for any programmer.
examples: Subclasses *override* the default constructor when they need extra fields.
He *overrode* the equals method but forgot to update the hash.
The child class *has overridden* three of the parent's methods.

oversee.gloss: To be in charge of work being done by other people and make sure it goes right.

senses.head: Supervise, be in charge of
senses.body: The only common sense. It implies broad responsibility rather than hands-on work — you *oversee* a project but your team does it.
examples: Two engineers *oversee* the whole assembly line.
She *oversaw* the renovation from the first permit to the last inspection.
The agency *has overseen* clinical trials like this for decades.
A federal monitor *had overseen* the department for three years by then.

senses.head: See without being noticed
senses.body: Archaic and now literary, meaning to catch sight of something you were not meant to see. Do not confuse it with *overlook*, which means to miss something.
examples: He *oversaw* the whole quarrel from the top of the stairs.
What she *had overseen* through the window she never repeated to anyone.

overtake.gloss: To catch up with and pass something, or, of an event or feeling, to come upon someone suddenly.

senses.head: Catch up and pass
senses.body: Used of vehicles, runners, and anything moving. In American English drivers usually say *pass*; *overtake* is the normal word in British driving and in race reporting on both sides.
examples: Faster riders *overtake* the pack on the final climb.
A gray sedan *overtook* us just before the bridge.
She *has overtaken* two runners since the last mile marker.

senses.head: Surpass in amount or rank
senses.body: Figurative, about numbers, sales, or standing rather than motion. Very common in business and statistics writing.
examples: Streaming revenue will *overtake* ticket sales within a few years.
China *overtook* Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
Online orders *have overtaken* walk-in business at both locations.

senses.head: Come upon suddenly (of events, feelings)
senses.body: The subject is a storm, an emotion, exhaustion, or events in general, and it is often passive: *overtaken by events*. Always something the person did not control.
examples: Panic can *overtake* even an experienced diver.
Exhaustion *overtook* him halfway up the trail.
The expedition *was overtaken* by a blizzard on the second day.
Their careful plan *had been overtaken* by events long before the vote.

senses.head: Overtake (British driving)
senses.body: In British road signs and driving rules *overtake* is the fixed term for passing another car — *no overtaking*. American road signs say *do not pass* instead, so the word carries a distinctly British flavor in this context.
examples: British learners are taught never to *overtake* on a blind bend.
The lorry *overtook* the coach on a stretch marked with solid white lines.

overthrow.gloss: To remove a government or system from power by force, or to overturn something established.

senses.head: Remove from power by force
senses.body: The central political sense — a coup, a revolution, an uprising. The object is a ruler, a government, or a regime.
examples: Rebel officers tried to *overthrow* the president in 1974.
A general strike *overthrew* the military junta within weeks.
The monarchy *has been overthrown* twice in a single century.
By spring the junta *had overthrown* the elected assembly.

senses.head: Overturn a system or idea
senses.body: Figurative and formal: a discovery or argument destroys an accepted framework. Common in writing about science and law.
examples: A single clean experiment can *overthrow* a theory that stood for decades.
Her findings *overthrew* the accepted timeline of the migration.
Digital tools *have overthrown* the old hierarchy of the newsroom.

senses.head: Throw past the target (sports)
senses.body: In baseball and football, to throw the ball beyond the player who was supposed to catch it. Domain-specific but common in game commentary.
examples: Young pitchers often *overthrow* the cutoff man when they rush.
The shortstop *overthrew* first base and let in the tying run.
He *had overthrown* his receiver on three straight plays.

overwrite.gloss: To write over something that was already there, replacing it — most often data in a file.

senses.head: Replace existing data
senses.body: The dominant modern sense, from computing: new content destroys the old content in the same place. What is overwritten is gone unless it was backed up.
examples: Do not *overwrite* the config file until you have a copy.
The installer *overwrote* my custom settings.
Someone *has overwritten* last night's export with an empty file.
By the time we noticed, the backup script *had overwritten* two weeks of logs.

senses.head: Write on top of existing writing
senses.body: The literal, physical sense — ink over ink, chalk over chalk. Used of manuscripts, forms, and whiteboards.
examples: Medieval scribes would *overwrite* older parchment to save material.
She *overwrote* the wrong date in heavier pen.
A later hand *had overwritten* several lines of the original text.

senses.head: Write in an overblown style
senses.body: Nearly always met as the participle used as an adjective — *overwritten prose*. It criticizes writing that is too elaborate for its subject.
examples: First novels are *overwritten* more often than they are underwritten.
The critic said the middle chapters *were badly overwritten*.
Editors warn students not to *overwrite* a simple scene.
Her workshop leader *had overwritten* every scene in his own draft.

partake.gloss: To take part in something, to eat or drink one's share of it, or, formally, to have some quality of it.

senses.head: Partake of — eat or drink
senses.body: Formal or jokingly formal, always with *of*. In everyday speech Americans say *have* or *help yourself to*; *partake* survives in toasts, menus, and dry humor.
examples: Guests are welcome to *partake* of the buffet after the ceremony.
He *partook* of the wine rather more freely than the others.
None of us *had partaken* of anything since breakfast.

senses.head: Partake in — take part in
senses.body: A formal alternative to *take part in* or *participate in*, used with an activity. Slightly stiff in ordinary conversation.
examples: Students may *partake* in the ceremony without walking across the stage.
Only a handful of villagers *partook* in the vote.
She *has partaken* in every fundraiser since the club opened.

senses.head: Partake of — have a quality
senses.body: Literary and formal: something shares in the nature of something else. The object is an abstract noun, and it is never used of people eating.
examples: His speeches *partake* of both the sermon and the stump speech.
The old house *partook* of a grandeur the street had long lost.
Her paintings *have partaken* of that stillness from the very beginning.

redraw.gloss: To draw something again in a changed form, whether a picture, a boundary, or the terms of a deal.

senses.head: Draw again, revise a drawing
senses.body: The plain literal sense, used of sketches, plans, and anything on screen that a program repaints.
examples: Please *redraw* the elevation with the new window heights.
He *redrew* the whole panel after the editor's note.
By Friday the architect *had redrawn* the second floor twice.

senses.head: Redraw boundaries or a map
senses.body: Political and administrative, about district lines, borders, or territory. Frequently figurative: an event *redraws the map* of an industry.
examples: State legislatures *redraw* congressional districts after every census.
The 1919 treaties *redrew* the map of central Europe.
Cheap batteries *have redrawn* the energy landscape.

senses.head: Redraw a bill or funds (finance)
senses.ru: выставить обратный вексель; повторно снять средства
senses.body: A banking term: to draw a fresh bill of exchange back on a drawer whose bill was dishonored, and, in some mortgage products, to take back extra payments you had already made. Technical and rare outside finance.
examples: The exporter may *redraw* on the buyer for the unpaid balance plus charges.
The bank *redrew* on its correspondent in London.
They *have redrawn* nearly all of the extra payments made last year.

regrow.gloss: To grow again after being cut, lost, or destroyed, or to make something grow again.

senses.head: Grow back (intransitive)
senses.body: The usual sense: hair, leaves, nerves, or forest returning on its own after loss.
examples: Lizard tails *regrow*, but never quite the way they were.
Her hair *regrew* within a year of the treatment.
The prairie grass *has regrown* over the burn scar.
By the second spring the hedge *had regrown* above the fence line.

senses.head: Grow again (transitive)
senses.body: With an object — a person or a lab makes something grow back. Common in horticulture and in tissue-engineering writing.
examples: You can *regrow* scallions from the roots in a glass of water.
Researchers *regrew* the cartilage on a printed scaffold.
The town *has regrown* its tree canopy since the storm.

retake.gloss: To take something again — a place captured back, an exam sat a second time, a shot filmed over.

senses.head: Recapture, take back
senses.body: Military and competitive: to win back a position, city, or lead that had been lost.
examples: Their plan was to *retake* the ridge before dawn.
Allied forces *retook* the port in a single night.
The team *has retaken* first place in the division.
By August the army *had retaken* most of the province.

senses.head: Take a test or course again
senses.body: Everyday academic use. American students *retake* the SAT; the noun is *a retake*.
examples: Most students *retake* the exam at least once.
He *retook* chemistry over the summer.
She *has retaken* the driving test three times.

senses.head: Film a scene again
senses.body: From film and photography: to shoot the same material over because the first attempt failed.
examples: The director wanted to *retake* the whole dinner scene.
They *retook* the final shot after the light changed.
The crew *had retaken* that entrance eleven times.

senses.head: Regain control or possession
senses.ru: вернуть себе, снова взять под контроль
senses.body: Figurative, about control, initiative, or property returning to its earlier holder.
examples: Shareholders moved to *retake* control of the board.
The lender *retook* possession of the building.
She *has retaken* the initiative in every negotiation since.

rewrite.gloss: To write something again in a different form, or to change what was previously established.

senses.head: Write again, revise
senses.body: The core sense: producing a new version of a text. Stronger than *edit* — a rewrite starts over rather than patching.
examples: I *rewrite* the opening paragraph more times than the rest of the piece.
She *rewrote* the ending after the first table read.
By the deadline he *had rewritten* every chapter but the last.

senses.head: Rewrite the rules, history, record books
senses.body: A set of fixed figurative phrases. *Rewrite history* can be neutral (new evidence) or accusatory (distorting the past); context decides.
examples: A single find can *rewrite* the history of the region.
That season *rewrote* the record books for the franchise.
Officials *have rewritten* the rules three times this year.

senses.head: Rewrite code
senses.body: Standard in software: replacing an implementation rather than fixing it. Often contrasted with *refactor*, which preserves the existing structure.
examples: We should *rewrite* the parser instead of patching it again.
They *rewrote* the backend in Go over one quarter.
The team *has rewritten* that module from scratch twice.

ride.gloss: To sit on and control a horse, bike, or motorcycle, to travel in a vehicle, or, figuratively, to depend on or endure something.

senses.head: Ride a horse
senses.body: The oldest sense and still the default when no vehicle is named. *Ride* here can be transitive (*ride a mare*) or intransitive (*she rides every weekend*).
examples: She *rides* every Saturday at a stable outside town.
He *rode* bareback across the pasture.
I *have ridden* that gray mare since she was three.
None of the kids *had ridden* a horse before that summer.

senses.head: Ride a bike or motorcycle
senses.body: Anything you sit astride takes *ride*, not *drive* — a motorcycle is *ridden* even though it has an engine.
examples: Most of the staff *ride* bikes to work.
He *rode* his motorcycle from Denver to the coast.
She *has ridden* the same road bike for a decade.

senses.head: Travel as a passenger
senses.body: Americans *ride* the bus, the subway, an elevator, or in the back seat. British English prefers *take the bus*, and *ride in a car* means being a passenger, never driving.
examples: I *ride* the train into the city three days a week.
We *rode* the elevator to the top floor in silence.
He *has ridden* that same commuter line for twenty years.

senses.head: Ride waves, wind, current
senses.body: Used of surfers, birds, and boats moving on water or air, and of anything carried along by a current. Also of a ship *riding at anchor*.
examples: Gulls *ride* the updrafts along the cliff without a wingbeat.
The little boat *rode* the swell better than we expected.
Surfers *have ridden* this break since the fifties.

senses.head: Be riding on — depend on
senses.ru: зависеть от, быть поставленным на карту
senses.body: Almost always in the continuous with an abstract subject: money, jobs, or a reputation *is riding on* an outcome. A fixed pattern rather than a free use.
examples: A lot of money *is riding on* the outcome of this hearing.
His whole reputation *rode on* one paragraph in that report.
Too much *has ridden on* this single account for too long.

senses.head: Ride out — get through safely
senses.body: To survive a storm, a downturn, or a scandal by holding on until it passes. The object is a period of trouble.
examples: Small firms rarely *ride out* a downturn this long.
They *rode out* the hurricane in the basement.
The company *has ridden out* worse quarters than this one.

senses.head: Ride someone — nag, pressure
senses.body: Informal American English: to criticize or push a person relentlessly. Always with a person as the object.
examples: Don't *ride* him about the mistake — he already knows.
The coach *rode* the rookies all through camp.
Her supervisor *has ridden* her about the same report for weeks.

rise.gloss: To move upward, to increase, to get up, or to advance in position — always without an object.

senses.head: Move upward
senses.body: The literal sense, used of smoke, the sun, water, or land. It never takes an object — you *raise* a thing, but a thing *rises* by itself.
examples: Steam *rises* off the pavement after a summer storm.
The moon *rose* behind the ridge just after nine.
The river *has risen* two feet since midnight.
By morning the water *had risen* over the doorsill.

senses.head: Increase in amount
senses.body: Used of prices, temperatures, numbers, and levels. Neutral and extremely common in news and business writing.
examples: Rents *rise* faster here than wages do.
Unemployment *rose* sharply in the fall.
Costs *have risen* every year since the merger.

senses.head: Get up from bed
senses.body: Formal or literary for people; *get up* is the everyday choice. It survives in fixed contexts: *all rise* in a courtroom, *rise and shine*, *rise early*.
examples: Farmers here *rise* before five most of the year.
The whole room *rose* when the judge came in.
He *had risen* and dressed before anyone else was awake.

senses.head: Advance in rank or standing
senses.body: About careers and reputations, often with *to* or *through*: *rise to the top*, *rise through the ranks*.
examples: Few analysts *rise* to partner in under a decade.
She *rose* through the ranks from dispatcher to chief.
He *has risen* from stock clerk to regional manager.

senses.head: Rise up — rebel
senses.body: Political, usually *rise up against* a ruler or a system. Formal and a little dramatic in tone.
examples: When the tax was announced, whole provinces *rose* against the crown.
The peasants *rose up* in the spring of that year.
The city *has risen* against its own council twice in living memory.

senses.head: Rise to the occasion
senses.body: A fixed idiom: to meet a difficult moment with unexpected strength. Also *rise to the challenge* and *rise above* (refuse to be dragged down by pettiness).
examples: Nobody knows who will *rise* to the occasion until the day comes.
She *rose* to the challenge and finished the season as captain.
He *has risen* above worse insults than that one.

senses.head: Dough, land, a river's source
senses.body: Three related specialized uses: bread dough swells, land slopes upward, and a river *rises* in the place where it begins.
examples: Let the dough *rise* for an hour in a warm kitchen.
The land *rose* steeply behind the barn.
The Rhine *rises* in the Swiss Alps.
The loaves *had risen* well past the rim of the pans.

see.gloss: To perceive with the eyes, and, by extension, to understand, to meet, to experience, or to make sure of something.

senses.head: Perceive with the eyes
senses.body: The base sense. It describes perception, not deliberate attention, so it is normally not used in the continuous: *I see it*, not *I am seeing it*.
examples: I *see* three deer at the edge of the field.
She *saw* the taillights turn onto the gravel road.
Nobody *has seen* that comet since 1997.
He *had seen* the letter long before he admitted it.

senses.head: Understand, grasp
senses.body: Very common, from *I see* as an acknowledgment to *see the point*. The object is an idea rather than a thing.
examples: I *see* what you mean about the second paragraph.
It took a week before anyone *saw* the flaw in the argument.
Now that you explain it, I *have* finally *seen* the logic of it.

senses.head: Meet with, consult
senses.body: Used of appointments and visits — *see a doctor*, *see a client*. The professional you consult is the object.
examples: You should *see* a doctor about that cough.
I *saw* my lawyer on Tuesday about the lease.
She *has seen* three specialists and gotten three answers.

senses.head: Be seeing someone — date
senses.body: Romantic, and one of the few uses of *see* that does take the continuous. *Are you seeing anyone?* is the standard way to ask about someone's relationship status.
examples: They *have been seeing* each other since March.
She *was seeing* somebody from the office at the time.
He does not *see* anyone seriously these days.

senses.head: Watch a movie, game, or show
senses.body: For a one-time event you *see* a film or a game; for regular viewing of television you *watch*. *Have you seen it?* is the standard question about a movie.
examples: Let's *see* the late show instead.
We *saw* the Cubs play in the rain.
I *have seen* that movie four times.

senses.head: See to it — make sure
senses.body: A fixed pattern for taking responsibility that something happens: *see to it that*, *see that*, or *see to* a task.
examples: Please *see* that the doors are locked at closing.
The super *saw to* the leak the same afternoon.
Someone *has seen to* the paperwork already.

senses.head: Witness, experience (of a period)
senses.ru: видеть, знавать, быть свидетелем (об эпохе, месте)
senses.body: The subject is a period, a place, or a thing rather than a person: *the decade saw enormous change*. Standard in journalism and history writing.
examples: The next ten years will *see* the whole industry reorganized.
The 1990s *saw* a wave of small presses open and close.
This town *has seen* three floods since I moved here.

senses.head: See someone off, see someone home
senses.body: To go with a person to their point of departure or destination. *See off* is at a station or airport; *see home* is walking someone back.
examples: We always *see* the grandparents off at the gate.
He *saw* her home through the rain.
The whole family *had seen* him off at the pier.

senses.head: See through — not be fooled
senses.body: Two related fixed uses: *see through* a person or a lie means you are not deceived; *see something through* means you stay with a task to the end.
examples: Voters *see through* that kind of promise immediately.
She *saw* the project *through* despite losing half her staff.
He *has seen through* every excuse I have ever offered.

senses.head: See as, see in — regard
senses.body: With *as* it means consider or interpret; with *in* it asks what quality someone finds attractive or promising in another.
examples: I *see* the delay *as* a chance to test it properly.
Critics *saw* the film *as* an apology for the war.
I never *saw* what she *saw* in him.
Investors *have seen* real potential *in* the smaller markets.

shake.gloss: To move quickly back and forth, to tremble, or to unsettle someone badly.

senses.head: Move something back and forth
senses.body: Transitive and literal — bottles, blankets, trees, a fist. This is the sense behind the label on medicine bottles.
examples: *Shake* the bottle well before pouring.
He *shook* the sand out of his shoes.
The wind *has shaken* the last apples loose.
Someone *had shaken* the vending machine hard enough to dent it.

senses.head: Tremble, vibrate
senses.body: Intransitive: the subject moves on its own, from cold, fear, laughter, or a passing train.
examples: My hands *shake* whenever I have to speak in public.
The whole house *shook* when the truck went by.
The windows *have shaken* like that since the mine reopened.

senses.head: Shake hands
senses.body: A fixed social use, alone or with *on it* to mark an agreement: *let's shake on it*.
examples: In this business you *shake* hands and the deal is done.
They *shook* hands and never spoke again.
We *had shaken* on the price before the paperwork arrived.

senses.head: Shake one's head
senses.body: Another fixed collocation. In American culture shaking the head means no or disbelief, and nodding means yes.
examples: He just *shakes* his head whenever the topic comes up.
She *shook* her head and went back to her book.
The doctor *had shaken* his head before saying a word.

senses.head: Upset, unsettle
senses.body: Figurative, about emotions and confidence. Very often passive — *she was badly shaken* — and also used of shaking someone's faith or belief.
examples: Bad reviews do not *shake* him at all.
The accident *shook* everyone on the crew.
Her confidence *has been shaken* by two rejections in a row.

senses.head: Shake off — get rid of
senses.body: To free yourself from an illness, a mood, a follower, or a defender. Common in both everyday speech and sports commentary.
examples: I cannot *shake off* this cold.
He *shook off* the tackler and went in for the score.
She *has* never quite *shaken off* the reputation she got that year.

senses.head: Shake up — reorganize; jolt
senses.body: Two senses of the same phrasal verb: to reorganize an institution drastically, or to shock a person. The noun *a shake-up* comes from the first.
examples: New owners always *shake up* the front office.
The near miss *shook* him *up* more than he let on.
Management *has shaken up* the department twice this year.

slay.gloss: To kill violently, in older and literary language; in modern slang, to impress or amuse enormously.

senses.head: Kill violently
senses.body: Literary, biblical, or heroic in tone — dragons, giants, and enemies are *slain*. Modern news writing keeps it mainly in headlines, where it is short for *murdered*.
examples: In the old stories a single knight can *slay* a dragon.
He *slew* the giant with a stone from the brook.
Thousands *had been slain* before the treaty was signed.
Two brothers *have been slain* on the same block this year.

senses.head: Amuse or impress hugely
senses.body: Informal: *you slay me* means you are hilarious, and a performer who *slays* an audience wins it completely. Older slang, but still widely understood.
examples: That story *slays* me every time you tell it.
Her opening set *slew* the crowd at the small club.
The comic *has slain* tougher rooms than this one.

senses.head: Slay — excel (modern slang)
senses.body: Recent slang, especially about fashion and performance: to look or perform outstandingly. In this sense the past is normally the regular *slayed*, not *slew* — the strong forms belong to the older senses.
examples: She *slays* every time she walks a runway.
They absolutely *slayed* that dance number.
He has *slayed* on that stage before.

smite.gloss: To strike a heavy blow, in archaic and biblical language; in living use, mostly as *smitten* — struck by love or by affliction.

senses.head: Be smitten with — infatuated
senses.body: By far the most common modern use, and only in the passive participle: *smitten with* or *smitten by* someone. Light and slightly playful in tone.
examples: He *was smitten* with her from the first rehearsal.
Anyone who meets that puppy *is smitten* immediately.
She *had been smitten* long before she admitted it to anyone.

senses.head: Strike hard
senses.body: Archaic and biblical, or used for humorous effect. The object is a person or an enemy, and the striker is often God or fate.
examples: The old text warns that the wicked will *smite* one another.
He *smote* the table with his fist and walked out.
The angel *had smitten* the camp before morning.

senses.head: Afflict, strike down
senses.body: Formal or literary, of disease, guilt, or disaster falling on someone. Nearly always passive: *smitten by plague*, *smitten with remorse*.
examples: Plague can *smite* a whole village in a season.
Conscience *smote* him halfway home.
The region *has been smitten* by drought three years running.

stride.gloss: To walk with long, decisive steps.

senses.head: Walk with long steps
senses.body: The main sense, and it carries confidence or purpose — you do not *stride* aimlessly. The participle *stridden* is rare enough that writers often rephrase to avoid it.
examples: He tends to *stride* rather than walk when he is angry.
She *strode* to the front of the room without a note in her hand.
The coach *has stridden* up and down that sideline for thirty seasons.
By then he *had stridden* halfway across the lobby.

senses.head: Stride over, stride across
senses.body: With a preposition it describes covering ground or stepping over an obstacle in one long step.
examples: Long-legged birds *stride* across the mudflats at low tide.
He *strode* over the fallen branch without breaking pace.
The hikers *had stridden* across three fields before noon.

senses.head: Stand astride, dominate
senses.body: Literary and now rare: to stand with a leg on either side of something, or figuratively to dominate it. Modern writing usually chooses *bestride* or *straddle* here instead.
examples: In the old cartoons the magnate seems to *stride* the whole continent.
The colossus *strode* the harbor mouth in the legend.

strive.gloss: To make great and sustained effort toward something difficult.

senses.head: Make a great effort, aim at
senses.body: Formal, used with *to* plus a verb or with *for* plus a goal. It implies long effort against difficulty, so it does not fit small everyday tasks. Both *strove* and the regular *strived* are accepted in American English; *strove* sounds more literary.
examples: Small clinics *strive* to keep costs down without cutting hours.
She *strove* for accuracy even when nobody was checking.
He *has striven* for that title since he was a teenager.
They *had striven* for years to keep the mill open.

senses.head: Contend, struggle against
senses.body: Older and more literary: to fight or compete with someone, usually with *against* or *with*. Rare in modern speech.
examples: Reformers had to *strive* against a century of habit.
The two houses *strove* with each other for a generation.
The settlers *had striven* against that river every spring.

take.gloss: To get hold of something, carry it, accept it, require it, or use it — the widest-ranging verb in this group.

senses.head: Get hold of, pick up
senses.body: The base physical sense: your hand closes on something. It also covers taking what is not yours, which is why *take* borders on *steal*.
examples: *Take* a napkin from the pile by the door.
She *took* the keys off the hook and left.
Someone *has taken* my umbrella from the stand.
By then the thieves *had taken* everything but the furniture.

senses.head: Carry or bring somewhere
senses.body: Movement away from where the speaker is — you *take* things there and *bring* them here. The direction is what separates the two verbs.
examples: I *take* the kids to school on my way in.
He *took* the package to the post office.
The neighbors *have taken* our mail inside all week.

senses.head: Require (time, effort, qualities)
senses.body: Very common with time — *it takes an hour* — and with abstract requirements: *it takes patience*, *it takes two*. The subject is usually the empty *it*.
examples: It *takes* about twenty minutes to get downtown.
The repair *took* longer than the estimate said.
It *has taken* three years to get the permits.

senses.head: Accept, receive
senses.body: Used of jobs, offers, advice, payment, and criticism. *We take cards* is the standard sign in an American store.
examples: Most food trucks here *take* cards now.
She *took* the job in Seattle after all.
He *has* never *taken* advice from anyone.

senses.head: Consume (medicine, food, drink)
senses.body: Standard with pills and doses, and with drugs in the negative sense. With food and drink it is a little formal — *take a little soup*.
examples: *Take* two of these with food.
He *took* his medication late and slept badly.
She *has taken* the same prescription for years.

senses.head: Travel by, use a route
senses.body: You *take* a bus, a cab, a flight, a highway, or the next exit. It covers both the vehicle and the road.
examples: I *take* the express bus when the weather is bad.
We *took* the coast road instead of the interstate.
They *have taken* that same flight every Monday.

senses.head: Study a subject; sit an exam
senses.body: American academic use: you *take* a class and *take* a test. British English says *sit* an exam and *do* a course.
examples: Freshmen *take* two writing courses their first year.
She *took* organic chemistry in the summer session.
He *has taken* the bar exam twice.

senses.head: Light-verb uses: take a break
