senses.body: *Take* combines with many action nouns to name the action itself: *take a look, a walk, a shower, a break, a picture, a nap, notes, a seat*. The meaning lives in the noun, not the verb.
examples: Let's *take* a break before the next session.
He *took* a picture of the whole crew on the last day.
She *has taken* careful notes at every meeting.

senses.head: Regard, interpret
senses.body: Usually with *as* or in fixed frames: *take it as a compliment*, *take her seriously*, *take it that*. It is about how you read something, not about handling it.
examples: Please do not *take* this the wrong way.
They *took* his silence as agreement.
I *had taken* her question for a joke until I saw her face.

senses.head: Take off
senses.ru: снимать (одежду); взлетать; уходить; резко пойти вверх
senses.body: Four common senses on one phrasal verb: remove clothing, leave the ground, leave abruptly (informal), and suddenly succeed. Context separates them easily.
examples: Please *take off* your shoes at the door.
The flight *took off* forty minutes late.
Sales *have taken off* since the review came out.

senses.head: Take after — resemble a relative
senses.body: Only about family, and about looks or character rather than behavior in a single moment. Never used of things.
examples: The younger boy *takes after* his mother's side.
She *took after* her grandfather in temperament more than in looks.
None of the kids *have taken after* him in music.

senses.head: Take over, take on, take up
senses.ru: брать на себя, перенимать; нанимать; заняться (чем-л.)
senses.body: Three high-frequency phrasal verbs: *take over* means assume control of something someone else ran; *take on* means accept a task or hire someone; *take up* means start a hobby or occupy space or time.
examples: A larger firm will *take over* the accounts in the fall.
She *took on* two new clients this month.
He *took up* the guitar at forty.
The reorganization *has taken up* most of the quarter.

test-drive.gloss: To drive a vehicle before buying it, or, loosely, to try anything out before committing to it.

senses.head: Drive a car before buying
senses.body: The literal sense, from car sales. Written with a hyphen and inflected on the second element: *test-drove*, *test-driven*.
examples: You should *test-drive* it on the highway, not just around the lot.
We *test-drove* three hybrids on Saturday.
That model *has been test-driven* by half the neighborhood.
By closing time he *had test-driven* everything on the lot.

senses.head: Try something out
senses.body: Figurative and informal, used of software, ideas, arguments, or anything you sample before adopting it.
examples: Let's *test-drive* the new scheduling tool for a week.
She *test-drove* the joke on her sister before the toast.
The team *has test-driven* two different workflows this month.

thrive.gloss: To grow strongly and do well — of people, businesses, plants, and animals.

senses.head: Flourish, do well
senses.body: Used of businesses, communities, and people. In American English the past is far more often the regular *thrived*; *throve* and *thriven* are older strong forms that survive mainly in literary writing.
examples: Small bookstores *thrive* in this part of the city.
The shop *throve* for twenty years under her father.
The cooperative *has thriven* despite two recessions.
By the war's end the port *had thriven* beyond anyone's expectation.

senses.head: Grow vigorously (plants, animals)
senses.body: The biological sense: healthy growth in good conditions. The medical phrase *failure to thrive* describes an infant who is not gaining weight normally.
examples: Basil *thrives* in a sunny window.
The transplanted seedlings *throve* after the first rain.
Nothing *has thriven* in that shady corner of the yard.

senses.head: Thrive on — need and enjoy
senses.body: A fixed pattern: a person does well precisely because of something others would find hard — pressure, chaos, attention.
examples: Some traders genuinely *thrive* on that kind of pressure.
She *throve* on deadlines her whole career.
He *has thriven* on being underestimated.

throw.gloss: To send something through the air from your hand, and, figuratively, to put, host, or unsettle.

senses.head: Send through the air
senses.body: The core sense, from a ball to a stone to a punch. In baseball the pitcher *throws*; in football the quarterback *throws* the ball.
examples: Kids *throw* rocks into that creek all summer.
He *threw* the ball over the catcher's head.
She *has thrown* out the first pitch twice.
Someone *had thrown* a brick through the front window.

senses.head: Put or move roughly, thrust
senses.body: Sudden or careless placement, literal or figurative: *throw your coat on the bed*, *throw him in jail*, *throw yourself into the work*.
examples: Just *throw* your bags in the back seat.
The judge *threw* him in jail for the weekend.
She *has thrown* herself into the campaign since January.

senses.head: Host an event
senses.body: Informal but completely standard American usage, mostly with *party*: *throw a party*, *throw a shower*, *throw someone a birthday dinner*.
examples: They *throw* a block party every Fourth of July.
We *threw* her a surprise dinner for her fiftieth.
The department *has thrown* a going-away party for everyone who leaves.

senses.head: Confuse, unsettle
senses.ru: сбивать с толку, выбивать из колеи
senses.body: Informal: an unexpected question or event throws a person. The object is a person, and it turns up most often in the past — *that threw me*.
examples: A question like that can *throw* even a prepared witness.
The change of venue *threw* the whole team.
Nothing in the interview *had thrown* her until that point.

senses.head: Throw up — vomit
senses.body: The ordinary everyday word for vomiting in American English; *vomit* itself sounds clinical. *Throw up* can also mean to build hastily, but the illness sense dominates.
examples: The motion of the boat makes some passengers *throw up*.
He *threw up* twice on the drive home.
She *has thrown up* every morning this week.

senses.head: Throw away, throw out — discard
senses.body: Literal for trash and figurative for wasted chances: *throw away an opportunity*. *Throw out* also means to eject a person or to reject a case.
examples: Please do not *throw away* the packing slip.
He *threw out* every box in the garage.
The judge *has thrown out* the entire complaint.

senses.head: Throw off — shed; mislead
senses.body: To get rid of something clinging — an illness, a mood, a pursuer — or to send someone in the wrong direction.
examples: A hot shower helps me *throw off* a headache.
The false trail *threw off* the search party for a day.
He *has* finally *thrown off* the flu.

senses.head: Throw in — add for free
senses.ru: добавить в придачу; сдаться (throw in the towel)
senses.body: A seller *throws in* an extra at no charge; separately, *throw in the towel* is a fixed idiom from boxing meaning to quit.
examples: The dealer will usually *throw in* floor mats.
They *threw in* a second charger with the phone.
After the third rejection he *had thrown in* the towel.

underbid.gloss: To offer a lower price than a competitor, or, in card games, to bid below the true strength of your hand.

senses.head: Bid lower than a rival
senses.ru: предложить более низкую цену, сбить цену
senses.body: Commercial: contractors *underbid* each other to win work. Note that in ordinary American business English the past and participle are simply *underbid*; the strong forms *underbade* and *underbidden* listed for this entry follow *bid — bade — bidden* and are archaic.
examples: Two firms tried to *underbid* us on the same contract.
The smaller shop *underbade* everyone and then could not finish the work.
We *have been underbidden* on every municipal job this year.
By the deadline they *had underbidden* the incumbent by nearly a third.

senses.head: Bid below your hand (cards)
senses.ru: заявить меньше, чем позволяет карта (в бридже)
senses.body: In bridge, to make a contract lower than your cards justify, giving away points you could have earned. Technical to card play.
examples: Cautious partners *underbid* good hands out of habit.
She *underbade* a hand worth an easy game.
He *has underbidden* twice tonight and it cost us the rubber.

underlie.gloss: To lie beneath something, either physically or as its hidden basis or cause.

senses.head: Be the basis or cause of
senses.body: The common sense, and it is abstract: an assumption, a principle, or a tension *underlies* an argument, a policy, or a conflict. Often met as the adjective *underlying*.
examples: Two assumptions *underlie* the entire proposal.
Old resentments *underlay* the whole dispute.
A simple idea *has underlain* the company's strategy from the start.
Fear of another shortage *had underlain* every decision that year.

senses.head: Lie physically underneath
senses.body: The literal geological or structural sense — one layer sits below another. Compare *overlie*, which is its exact mirror.
examples: Limestone beds *underlie* most of the county.
A layer of peat *underlay* the topsoil.
Solid granite *has underlain* the site all along.

undertake.gloss: To take on a task or responsibility, or to give a formal promise to do something.

senses.head: Take on, begin (a task)
senses.body: Formal, with a substantial object: a study, a project, a journey, a review. You do not *undertake* small errands.
examples: The agency will *undertake* a full review of the program.
They *undertook* the restoration without any public money.
The lab *has undertaken* three studies on the same question.
By spring the team *had undertaken* the largest survey in its history.

senses.head: Formally promise, commit
senses.body: Legal and contractual, with *to* plus a verb: a party *undertakes to* deliver, pay, or maintain. The noun *an undertaking* names the promise itself.
examples: The seller *undertakes* to deliver within thirty days.
He *undertook* to repay the loan in full by June.
The city *has undertaken* to maintain the trail in perpetuity.

senses.head: Arrange funerals
senses.body: The source of the noun *undertaker*, but the verb in this sense is now dated and rare; today one says *work as a funeral director*.
examples: The same firm *undertook* for most of the county in the 1890s.
His family *had undertaken* for three generations in that town.

underwrite.gloss: To accept financial risk for something — an insurance policy, a securities issue — or, more broadly, to pay for it.

senses.head: Assume insurance risk
senses.body: The original sense, from insurers signing their names under a policy. An *underwriter* decides whether the risk is acceptable and at what price.
examples: Few insurers will *underwrite* coastal property at that elevation now.
Lloyd's syndicates *underwrote* the voyage for a hefty premium.
The carrier *has underwritten* this fleet for a decade.
Nobody *had underwritten* a rig that far offshore before.

senses.head: Guarantee a securities issue
senses.body: Investment banking: a bank buys or guarantees an entire issue of stock or bonds and resells it, absorbing the risk that it does not sell.
examples: Two banks will *underwrite* the offering.
The firm *underwrote* the largest IPO of the year.
That syndicate *has underwritten* most of the state's bond issues.

senses.head: Fund, sponsor
senses.body: General and now very common, especially of foundations and public broadcasting: to pay for something and absorb any loss.
examples: A local foundation will *underwrite* the summer concerts.
Her employer *underwrote* the whole conference.
Listeners *have underwritten* this station since 1974.

undo.gloss: To unfasten something, to reverse an action, or, in older language, to ruin someone.

senses.head: Unfasten, untie, open
senses.body: The literal sense — buttons, laces, knots, zippers, packages. The opposite of *do up*.
examples: I cannot *undo* this knot with cold hands.
He *undid* the top button and loosened his tie.
Someone *has undone* the latch on the gate.
By the time we found the crate, the twine *had been undone*.

senses.head: Reverse an action
senses.body: Figurative and, since computers, everywhere: *undo the last change*, Ctrl+Z. Often in the pattern *cannot be undone*, meaning permanent.
examples: You can *undo* the last five edits with the arrow.
That single email *undid* six months of goodwill.
The new agreement *has undone* most of the damage.
Nothing *had undone* the harm of the first announcement.

senses.head: Ruin, destroy (a person)
senses.body: Formal and literary, and often passive: *he was undone by his own pride*. The old fixed cry *I am undone* means ruined.
examples: Vanity will *undo* a careful negotiator faster than bad luck.
His own memos *undid* him at the hearing.
The family *had been undone* by a single bad harvest.

senses.head: Come undone
senses.body: A fixed phrase with *come*: literally a knot or seam comes loose, figuratively a plan or a person falls apart.
examples: My shoelace *comes undone* every mile or so.
The whole schedule *came undone* after the second delay.
He *had come undone* well before the trial ended.

withdraw.gloss: To take something back or take it out, to move back from a place, or to become distant from people.

senses.head: Take money out
senses.body: Banking, and the first sense most learners meet. The noun is *a withdrawal*, and it is what an ATM performs.
examples: You can *withdraw* up to five hundred dollars a day.
She *withdrew* the whole balance and closed the account.
He *has withdrawn* money twice this week.
By Friday they *had withdrawn* nearly all of the deposit.

senses.head: Take back, retract
senses.body: Used of statements, offers, applications, charges, and products. Formal but common in news and business.
examples: I *withdraw* the question, Your Honor.
The company *withdrew* its offer after the inspection.
Prosecutors *have withdrawn* two of the charges.

senses.head: Pull out of, quit
senses.ru: выходить (из гонки, конкурса), отказываться от участия
senses.body: Intransitive with *from*: a candidate, a student, or a country stops taking part.
examples: Two candidates *withdraw* from the primary every cycle.
He *withdrew* from the tournament with a shoulder injury.
She *has withdrawn* from three classes this semester.

senses.head: Retreat, move back (troops, people)
senses.body: Both transitive (a general *withdraws* forces) and intransitive (troops *withdraw*). Also used of people leaving a room formally.
examples: The commander decided to *withdraw* the forward units.
The jury *withdrew* to deliberate just after four.
Peacekeepers *have withdrawn* from the eastern districts.

senses.head: Become distant, withdrawn
senses.body: Psychological, about a person retreating from contact. Most often met as the adjective *withdrawn* — a quiet, closed-off person.
examples: Teenagers sometimes *withdraw* from family entirely for a while.
He *withdrew* into his work after the divorce.
She *has withdrawn* from almost everyone she used to see.

senses.head: Withdraw from a drug
senses.body: Medical: to stop taking a substance the body has come to depend on. The noun *withdrawal* names the symptoms that follow.
examples: Patients should not *withdraw* from this medication abruptly.
He *withdrew* from nicotine over about six weeks.
She *has withdrawn* from the sedatives under supervision.

write.gloss: To form letters and words, to compose a text, and to communicate or record in writing.

senses.head: Form letters and words
senses.body: The physical act — pen on paper, chalk on a board. The classic learner trap sits here: not *I have wrote* but *I have written*.
examples: Kids *write* their names before they can read them.
He *wrote* the address on the back of a receipt.
She *has written* the same phrase on every page.
Someone *had written* the date in pencil in the corner.

senses.head: Compose a text or work
senses.body: The authorial sense: books, articles, reports, essays. Used intransitively, *she writes* can mean she is a writer by trade.
examples: He *writes* for two magazines and teaches on the side.
She *wrote* her first novel in a rented cabin.
They *have written* four reports on the same landfill.

senses.head: Write to someone, correspond
senses.body: American English allows *write me* as well as *write to me*; British English keeps the *to*. Used of letters and email alike.
examples: *Write* me when you get settled.
She *wrote* to her brother every Sunday for years.
He *has written* to the department three times without an answer.

senses.head: Write a check, write up
senses.body: To fill out a formal document: a check, a prescription, a ticket, an invoice. *Write up* also means to prepare a report or to cite someone formally.
examples: The clinic will *write* you a prescription today.
The officer *wrote* him a ticket for the expired tag.
Her manager *has written* her up twice for being late.

senses.head: Compose music
senses.body: Standard for songs, scores, and arrangements — you *write* a song the way you write a poem.
examples: She *writes* most of the band's material.
He *wrote* that melody in a single afternoon.
They *have written* together since high school.

senses.head: Write code; write data
senses.body: Two technical senses: programmers *write* software, and a program *writes* data to a disk or a file. Both are everyday vocabulary in computing.
examples: We *write* most of the tooling in Python.
The script *wrote* the results to a temporary file.
He *has written* every line of that parser himself.

senses.head: Write down, write off
senses.body: *Write down* means to record on paper. *Write off* has two senses: cancel a debt or reduce an asset's book value, and dismiss a person or thing as hopeless.
examples: *Write* it *down* before you forget the number.
The bank *wrote off* the remaining balance.
Critics *had written* him *off* years before his best season.
